title: Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence
summary: What AI is, how machines learn from data and where it is used. A short course with no programming, after which you receive a certificate.
description:
An introductory course for anyone who wants to understand what stands behind the words “artificial intelligence” and “machine learning”.

Three modules: history and core concepts, how models are trained, and applications and ethics. Each module ends with a short quiz and the course ends with a final exam. To receive a certificate you need to complete all lessons and pass all quizzes. No programming experience is required.
outcomes: Explain what artificial intelligence is and tell narrow AI from general AI
Describe how a model learns from data and name the three main types of learning
Recognise overfitting and explain why a model must be checked on new data
Assess the ethical risks of using AI: bias, privacy, accountability

modules.title: What is artificial intelligence
modules.description: A definition, a short history and the kinds of AI.

lessons.title: Definition and a short history
lessons.content:
**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is the field of computer science concerned with building programs that can solve tasks that normally require human intelligence: recognising speech and images, translating texts, making decisions.

## Key milestones

- **1950** — Alan Turing publishes “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” and proposes the test that bears his name.
- **1956** — at the Dartmouth workshop John McCarthy introduces the term “artificial intelligence”.
- **1997** — the chess program Deep Blue defeats world champion Garry Kasparov.
- **2016** — AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol at the game of Go.
- **2020s** — large language models learn to hold conversations and write texts.

Progress came in waves: periods of great expectations were followed by “AI winters”, when funding was cut because results did not live up to the promises.

lessons.title: Narrow and general AI
lessons.content:
All AI systems that exist today are **narrow AI**: they solve one specific task well and cannot transfer their skills to others.

## Kinds of AI

- **Narrow AI (ANI)** — a chess program, a recommendation system, a voice assistant. These systems do not understand the world; they find patterns in data.
- **General AI (AGI)** — a hypothetical system able to solve any intellectual task at a human level. It does not exist yet.
- **Superintelligence** — an even more hypothetical system that surpasses humans in every area.

When the news says “AI passed an exam” or “AI painted a picture”, it means narrow AI: very powerful, but specialised.

questions.prompt: In which year was the term “artificial intelligence” introduced at the Dartmouth workshop?
questions.explanation: John McCarthy proposed the term in 1956 while preparing the Dartmouth workshop.

questions.prompt: Which kind do all AI systems that exist today belong to?
questions.explanation: General AI (AGI) does not exist yet; all current systems are specialised.

questions.prompt: The chess program Deep Blue defeated world champion Garry Kasparov.

modules.title: How machines learn
modules.description: Data, features, models and the three types of learning.

lessons.title: Data, features and models
lessons.content:
In classical programming a person writes the rules and the computer follows them. In **machine learning** it is the other way round: a person provides examples and the program finds the rules itself.

## Core concepts

- **Data** — the examples the system learns from (emails, images, tables).
- **Feature** — a measurable characteristic of an example: the number of links in an email, the area of an apartment, a client's age.
- **Label** — the correct answer we want to predict: “spam” or “not spam”, the price of an apartment.
- **Model** — a mathematical function that produces a prediction from features.
- **Training** — tuning the model's parameters so that its predictions match the labels on the training data.

The quality of a model almost always comes down to the quality of the data: errors and skews in the data pass into the model.

lessons.title: Three types of learning
lessons.content:
## Supervised learning

The data contains correct answers (labels). The model learns to predict them. Examples: spam detection, price forecasting, handwritten digit recognition.

## Unsupervised learning

There are no labels; the model looks for structure on its own. Example: splitting customers into groups with similar behaviour (clustering).

## Reinforcement learning

An agent acts in an environment and receives a reward or a penalty. This is how game-playing programs and robots learn: they try, evaluate the result and improve their strategy.

lessons.title: Overfitting and model validation
lessons.content:
A model that has memorised the training examples perfectly may perform poorly on new data. This is called **overfitting**.

Imagine a student who has learned the exam answers by heart: they answer familiar questions perfectly but get lost at the slightest change of wording.

## How to protect against it

1. Split the data into **training** and **test** sets and measure quality only on the test set.
2. Use more varied data.
3. Choose a simpler model if a complex one overfits.

An honest evaluation is always made on data the model did not see during training.

questions.prompt: What is the correct answer that a model learns to predict called?
questions.explanation: A label is the target value for each example in the training data.

questions.prompt: Splitting customers into groups without predefined categories is an example of…
questions.explanation: There are no labels and the model finds the structure itself: this is unsupervised learning (clustering).
The model memorises the training examples instead of finding general patterns.
options: The model performs poorly on both training and new data
The model performs well on training data but poorly on new data
The model was trained for too little time

questions.prompt: Select all valid ways to fight overfitting.
questions.explanation: Testing on a held-out set, more varied data and a simpler model all help. Evaluating on training data does not reveal overfitting.
options: Evaluate quality on a test set
Evaluate quality on training data only

modules.title: AI in life and ethics
modules.description: Where AI is used and the questions of responsibility it raises.

lessons.title: Where AI is used
lessons.content:
AI systems are already built into everyday services:

- **Medicine** — analysing scans and supporting the doctor in making a diagnosis.
- **Transport** — navigation, traffic forecasts, driver-assistance systems.
- **Education** — adaptive trainers, automatic checking of assignments.
- **Agriculture** — analysing satellite images of fields, forecasting yields.
- **Banking and retail** — detecting fraud, recommending products.
- **Language** — machine translation, voice assistants, search.

In all these cases AI amplifies a person but does not replace responsibility for the decision.

lessons.title: Ethics, bias and accountability
lessons.content:
A model learns from data, so it repeats the skews in that data. If past hiring data favoured a particular group, the model may reproduce that bias.

## Key questions

- **Bias and fairness** — does the system work equally well for different groups of people?
- **Privacy** — what personal data is collected and how is it protected?
- **Explainability** — can we understand why the system made exactly this decision?
- **Accountability** — who is responsible for a mistake: the developer, the service owner, the user?

The principle of responsible use is simple: important decisions about people must not be made without human oversight and a way to appeal.

questions.prompt: Why can a model be biased?
questions.explanation: A model learns from data and reproduces the skews that are in it.
options: Because it learns from data that contains skews
Because the model invents the rules itself

questions.prompt: What does explainability of an AI system mean?
questions.explanation: Explainability is the ability to understand the reasons for a particular decision of the system.
options: We can understand why the system made exactly this decision
The system has an understandable interface

questions.prompt: Important decisions about people should be made without human involvement if the model is accurate.
questions.explanation: Even an accurate model makes mistakes. Important decisions require human oversight and a way to appeal.

questions.prompt: Who proposed a test for judging whether a machine has intelligence?
questions.explanation: Alan Turing described this test in his 1950 paper.
All current systems are narrow AI. General AI and superintelligence are still hypothetical.
options: General AI that solves any task
Narrow AI that solves specific tasks

questions.explanation: A feature is a measurable characteristic of an example from which the model makes its prediction.
options: The correct answer for an example
A measurable characteristic of an example
The result of testing a model

questions.prompt: In which tasks is reinforcement learning used?
questions.explanation: An agent gets a reward or a penalty for its actions: this is how game-playing programs and robots learn.
options: When there are labelled examples with answers
When an agent receives a reward or a penalty for its actions
When data needs to be split into groups

questions.prompt: To fairly evaluate a model's quality you need to use…
questions.explanation: Evaluating on data the model has not seen shows how it will work in reality.
options: Data the model did not see during training
Any data, it does not matter

questions.prompt: Select all questions that relate to the ethics of AI use.
questions.explanation: Bias, privacy and accountability are key ethical questions. The speed of an interface is not an ethical matter.
options: The colour scheme of the interface
